entries.title: ‘We left Ireland because there wasn’t work – and we wanted to get the hell away’: Trespasses author Louise Kennedy
entries.summary: Her Troubles-set debut became a hit TV series starring Gillian Anderson. Now the novelist has returned to her teen years for a follow-up. She talks about her journey from chef to author, and how her cancer diagnosis inspired her to writeLouise Kennedy’s life has hardly wanted for dramatic events, but the recent past has been spectacularly busy, even by her standards. entries.content:
Louise Kennedy’s life has hardly wanted for dramatic events, but the recent past has been spectacularly busy, even by her standards. You wouldn’t know it to look at her, as we chat in the sitting room of the house in Sligo that she shares with her husband, son and daughter, but this is the home that she once thought would be repossessed. The couple bought it “for stupid money” in 2007, when they also opened a restaurant, initially so successful that the only way seemed to be up. The following year, financial mayhem descended on Ireland, their customers ebbed away, and the Celtic Tiger years morphed into a country racked with job losses, bankruptcies, apparently endless debt. “I didn’t think I’d ever be able to keep the house,” she says, glancing around an elegant room dotted with beautiful objects and plants, but nonetheless relaxed and comfortable. “I’d say we only got out of negative equity about a month ago. There are probably arguments for moving now, but I’m so proud that we managed to hold on to it, I’m not going anywhere. I’m going to be carried out of here in a box.”

Kennedy had been a chef for 30 years, working all over the place from Dublin to London and, for two years, Beirut, before ending up in Sligo, on Ireland’s west coast, not far from the border with her native Northern Ireland. Crucially, she had never given a thought to writing, not since a teacher had admired a poem she wrote when she was seven. Now, she is about to publish her second novel, Stations, which follows a collection of short stories, The End of the World Is a Cul-de-Sac, and her debut, Trespasses, which was shortlisted for the 2023 Women’s prize for fiction and won other prizes in Ireland and the UK in 2022 and 2023. Last year, Trespasses gained further acclaim when it was adapted for Channel 4 in a production starring Gillian Anderson as the mother of Cushla, the young Catholic teacher who falls in love with Michael, an older, married Protestant lawyer, in 1970s Belfast.

Trespasses fired readers’ imaginations because it gave an already complex love story a terrifying, high-stakes backdrop; Michael and Cushla’s relationship wasn’t simply clandestine because it was extramarital, but because they came from communities pitted against one another in an occupied country. And to recreate the detail, texture and jeopardy of Belfast at the time, Kennedy had to look no further than her own upbringing.

She relates it so vividly and, at times, so humorously, that you have to remind yourself how intensely difficult it must have been. Kennedy’s Catholic family ran pubs in Belfast. One day, her grandmother was on her way to bank the takings when a bomb exploded in a building she was walking past and a chunk of glass pierced her jugular vein. “Some off-duty British soldier, a young fella who was down the town, held her neck together to stop her from bleeding to death until the ambulance came,” Kennedy recalls, before adding that her grandmother’s life was saved by the fur coat she’d been wearing. Throughout the ordeal, she wouldn’t let go of the handbag full of money, nor stop insisting she had to go and fetch her daughter from school.

“There was a lot of scarring on her face because she’d been cut by glass, but already, even in 71, the plastic surgeons in the north were just brilliant at patching people up. She just had very fine lines where the scarring was. She was really lucky.” What about psychologically? “She was a complete walking trauma case. She never talked about that. She wouldn’t even have known the word trauma. But if there was a loud noise, she’d go to pieces.”

Meanwhile, Kennedy’s father had experienced intimidation at work, in a factory in East Belfast where he was the only Catholic. He had been followed home, and one of their Catholic neighbours had been killed in a loyalist “romper room” – essentially, an interrogation and murder site, the slang taken from a children’s TV programme. Now, her father was training to become an accountant through evening correspondence courses, simultaneously studying and minding the children while his wife went to work in the pub. One night, Kennedy’s mother, grandmother, two uncles and a policeman found themselves standing in a tunnel opposite the building when it was blown up, an attack that found its way into Trespasses. “It was a crazy thing to happen. And I think that that was the thing about the north: you know it’s not normal, you know it’s mental, but yet it is normal because this is how you have to live. You just have to go on about your business, because otherwise you’re going to be freaking out left, right, and centre. ”

Kennedy’s skill at conjuring the past without succumbing to the shorthand of nostalgia was one of the qualities that made for the success of the adaptation of Trespasses, which was written by Ailbhe Keogan, who also worked on Bad Sisters. “Ailbhe is not from the north, she’s from Kerry, and she was very open to me. I wanted the dialogue to be authentic to the north, but not just to the north. It also had to sound like 1975, and that’s quite easy for me to remember: the voice in my head is of a child in the north of Ireland in the 70s. And people don’t speak the same now as they did then. The place is really different. It was quite a complicated location shoot for that reason, because a lot of the place was wrecked and a lot of rebuilding has been done since that. It was pretty tricky to try and find a bar that hasn’t changed at all. The book is set in Holywood, County Down, where I grew up, but Holywood doesn’t look like it did in the 70s, so it was filmed in Portaferry, a village in County Down.”

In 1979, life changed again. Kennedy was 12, and in her first year at grammar school, when her parents decided they’d had enough and uprooted the family to Naas, then a small town not far south of Dublin. She hated it. “From my point of view, it was really crap.” She lost her pals, it took two years to get the phone connected, and even worse, there was only one television station, “so all of my cultural references had been wiped out”. Six weeks later, they went back to Belfast for a visit, and Kennedy was shocked to find how strange a friend’s accent sounded to her. “I just thought ‘Oh my God! I don’t belong anywhere.’ I didn’t belong to either place, and I still feel that now. When you leave a place, it goes on about its business, but for me it’s frozen in time.”

Back then, though, she didn’t have that perspective. “I was an atrocious adolescent. I was really angry that we’d had to leave and move to a place where there was one TV channel.” And it’s this dislocation that she’s mined for her new novel, Stations, in which two misfit teenage protagonists, Róisín and Red, cleave together to create some version of belonging. But as the story progresses from the early 1980s to this century, moving from Ireland to London, it becomes apparent that only one of them will thrive.

It’s a portrait not only of teenage alienation, displacement and small-town Ireland, but of one of the waves of Irish emigration that have characterised its history. Remembering her own time in London, Kennedy says that you could walk into a pub on Sunday mornings in the 1980s and 90s and feel like you were at mass. And you could also feel that you were in flight: “We left because there wasn’t work, but we also left because it was a closed, judgmental, shithole theocracy that we were living in, and we wanted to get the hell away.” It’s that historical precision that has led Anne Enright to say of Stations that “it holds a national sorrow”, describing it as a “work of mourning and reclamation”.

And in Róisín, Kennedy gave herself permission to write a “pain in the arse” character, unpopular, temperamental, self-centred, in contrast to Cushla whom, she says, readers found so likable. “I ran into a friend of mine recently who was in school with me. She was asking what the book is about and I said a character who moved from the north, and everybody in school hates her. She was like, is it a memoir?”

Back to that wild pivot from cooking to writing. How did all this happen? Put simply, Kennedy was still trying to keep her ailing restaurant on its legs back in 2014 when she found herself ambushed into going along to a new creative writing group set up by the writer Una Mannion. “Why would I be doing that?” she asked the friend doing the persuading, visual artist Niamh Mac Cabe, whereupon Mac Cabe just turned up and plonked her in the car. “I thought it was the most hilarious thing I’d ever heard in my life,” Kennedy remembers. But at that first meeting of eight or so people, Kennedy found herself committing to writing a piece over the next few weeks. “From the minute that I started trying to write this mad little short story – I didn’t even know what a short story was really – I just thought: I don’t really care what happens as long as I can find a way to keep doing this.”

That story, which eventually found its way on to national radio, drew on a family memory, and told of a young girl in the 1920s who gets into a world of trouble when she writes Rudolph Valentino’s name in the list of that month’s deaths at church. When she read it to the group, “I fully expected everybody just to laugh or to very politely move on from having to talk about my crap story, but they were wildly enthusiastic. So I thought, ‘OK, I’m going to try to write another one.’”

Partly, she was enjoying the distraction. At work, Kennedy and her husband were constantly firefighting to stave off creditors and make sure staff got paid. “We were skint. Everybody was, and I suppose the thing is that if the whole country is like that, it means that the people who in the past you might have been able to go and borrow a couple of bob from didn’t have any. They were all up the shit as well.” When the restaurant finally closed, a few months after she had joined the writing group, “I just thought, I don’t care. I could sit and fart around trying to write something for two or three hours and I wouldn’t even have thought about the business.”

After that seismic change, her writing life began to blossom; she accumulated short stories, did an MA and then started a PhD at Queens University in Belfast, where she was supervised by the writer Garrett Carr, and began to publish in magazines. She acquired an agent, Eleanor Birne, who was building a list of Irish writers, and who told her that her work might be more attractive to British publishers if they thought a novel was coming. “I had lied to her and said, ‘Oh yeah, I’m kind of working on a novel’, but I wasn’t really.” She told Carr the same. But in fact, the idea for Trespasses was beginning to brew.

And then, another curve ball arrived, in the form of a diagnosis of melanoma: a mole on her shoulder blade had mutated into cancer, and subsequently, the cancer had spread. First, there was the prospect of surgery and, later, immunotherapy. She didn’t, she says, want to be thinking about cancer all the time, but she knew she wouldn’t be working as she had been. “So I just rigged myself up a sling. I sat here, off my tits on really strong painkillers for a few days and watched all three series of Call My Agent. But I couldn’t really do anything, so I thought, OK, the only thing I can do is sit at the kitchen table and try to write 1,000 words a day of something that might be a novel, and see what happens. So by the time I went back to work, I had 64,000 words of something. It wasn’t really a novel. It was a pile of shite. But when I did actually go back to it, there was something on the page to fix.”

Kennedy subsequently endured various complications and resurgences of her original cancer, including damage to her pituitary gland that caused sudden menopause and severe endocrine problems. She has spent several years tailoring her life around treatment – during our conversation, an alarm reminds her to take one of her many daily pills – but she’s on far more of an even keel nowadays. I ask her whether the next book will follow a chronological pattern and anchor itself in the 1990s; the answer is yes, and she’s working on it.

Although she says she prefers the doing to the being when it comes to literary life – in other words, writing rather than talking about it – she’s established herself enough to rule out a return to the kitchen. At least, not professionally: before I leave, she ushers me to the table and produces, with zero fanfare, a homemade quiche, homemade bread, homemade paté and, finally, a vast homemade raspberry and lemon curd cake. Every mouthful is delicious. You can entirely imagine that, had a global financial crisis not wrecked her career as a restaurateur, she would still have been cooking up a storm: good news for diners, but a major blow to readers.

entries.title: ‘My generation of novelists is dying’: Rose Tremain on 70 years of writing, and late-life inspiration
entries.summary: As her latest novel about Daphne du Maurier is published, the bestselling author reflects on age and creativity – and why at 83 she has no plans to stop My generation of writers is dying. Of Granta’s fabled list of 20 Best of Young British Novelists, 1983, six are gone, including our most princely satirist, Martin Amis. We’re all approaching birthdays where the cake is too small for the candles. S
entries.content:
My generation of writers is dying. Of Granta’s fabled list of 20 Best of Young British Novelists, 1983, six are gone, including our most princely satirist, Martin Amis. We’re all approaching birthdays where the cake is too small for the candles. Some of us are wounded: Salman Rushdie by an attacker’s knife, Julian Barnes lives with blood cancer, others with the fatal hurt of being forgotten.

But what’s the likely fate of those of us who are surviving – for now? Do readers still love us? When Barnes announced that he was signing off because of illness, was he also intuiting that the younger generations had heard enough from us old birds and geezers who were young when Sean Connery had dimples, when David Hockney first coloured his hair yellow?

The answer is probably “yes”. But here’s what I believe: contrary to what publishers hope and expect, serious writers don’t think obsessively about readers, or even about sales, royalties and prizes. What we talk to each other about, what we dream of, what we can’t live without is the work itself. When I endured a terrifying procedure for pancreatic cancer in 2019 and contemplated the likelihood of dying in Addenbrooke’s hospital, I spent wide-awake nights mourning not only the people I love and the places that are precious to me, but the end of storytelling. Ideas for stories have peopled my life since the age of 12, when I wrote my first play at boarding school. My existence devoid of these would definitely feel what Amis once called “thin”.

From interviews Hockney gave towards the end of his 88 years, when yellow had turned to white, we gleaned a fine understanding of the elderly artist’s unflagging commitment to a day-by-day engagement with his art. The simplicity of the Hockney philosophy – “I wake up. And I go to work” – enabled him to rival Picasso with the vastness and variety of his output. He lived and breathed painting. The idea that he would suddenly stop doing this he would surely have thought plain stupid, and I’m with him on that. Though there can be a falling-off in the work of artists and writers as they age, this is by no means inevitable; the reasons for keeping on are not too hard to find.

Certainly I’m getting towards the end of my life, but why should what remains of it be stricken by the loss of the one constant that has kept me company for 70 years, since that first little school play? To those who might imagine me in “retirement” tending my garden in Norfolk, existing only through this and through the lives of my daughter and my grandchildren, I need to explain that ideas for novels and stories still arrive in my head all the time, like supplicants at the gate. They beg to be let in. Where would all this clamour go if I shut them out?

This may be delusional, but I don’t believe the work done in the last third of my life is inferior to that done near its beginning. Critical reaction to my later novels – The Gustav Sonata (2016), Islands of Mercy (2020), Lily (2021) and Absolutely and Forever (2023) – was very positive and these books were written on the kind of creative high that I never experienced in my early writing days. In contrast, there were a few writers on the Granta 1983 list who had already foreseen a golden road ahead. Amis and McEwan seemed to arrive on the scene as fully fashioned geniuses, nudging literary fame in their 20s. Rushdie, too, had by then published his Booker sensation, Midnight’s Children, and was clearly a star.

The rest of us lined up in their wake. I’d published only two books and still felt uncertain that I really understood the form of the novel well enough to write anything worth keeping. I retreated back to play writing, this time for the BBC radio drama department, and was surprised to win an award for one of the best radio plays of 1984 for Temporary Shelter, starring the wonderful late Roy Kinnear (Rory’s Dad) as a naive English tourist facing up to the shortcomings of his life on a French campsite.

When, in 1988, I had the idea for my “breakthrough novel”, Restoration, I remember that I drew on one of the themes explored in Temporary Shelter: the protagonist as a shambling man who finds himself in a world he doesn’t understand and who makes a spectacular mess of things until he begins to learn the lessons his own nature is ready to teach him. But by this time I’d begun to learn lessons of my own about what kind of novel I wanted to write.

I inclined towards the epic rather than the miniature. History’s great canvas was a constant lure, yet my opinion on historical research is that it has to be done thoroughly and then almost abandoned, to let the imagination do its essential work. (Kipling described this process as lighting a great fire and then working only with its riddled embers.) Humour had to be part of the storytelling mix and could play a lovely melody above the bass notes of tragedy. Above all, I understood that to live with a work of fiction for the many months that it takes to complete it, one has to love it quite passionately and be comfortable with all its moods and habits, or – as Colm Tóibín puts it with delicious domestic flair – one has to stay for long periods of time in one’s “mental pyjamas”.

My mental pyjamas are on, then, but is it time to put everything to bed? This may be stubborn, but I don’t feel that it is. My latest project brings together both the young playwright that I once was and the elderly novelist I am now. The new book is titled The Housekeeper, and is a reimagining of the inspiration behind Daphne du Maurier’s classic novel Rebecca. It began as a short story in 2014, but I have now brought it to life not only as a novel but also as a screenplay for a film, directed by Richard Eyre and starring Anthony Hopkins and Helena Bonham Carter. I’ve been enthralled by the script work. It takes me back to standing in the wings of the school stage, hearing my own words spoken aloud for the first time.

entries.title: The best recent crime and thrillers – review roundup
entries.summary: Murder at the Grand Alpine Hotel by Lucy Foley; The Silent Appeal by Janice Hallett; Cold Sunset by William Boyd; The Occidental Book of the Dead by T Geronimo Johnson and The Last Tenant by Eva Björg ÆgisdóttirMurder at the Grand Alpine Hotel by Lucy Foley (HarperCollins, £22) This, the first Miss Marple continuation novel, must have been a more difficult undertaking than a new Hercule Poirot; fu
entries.content:
Murder at the Grand Alpine Hotel by Lucy Foley (HarperCollins, £22)

This, the first Miss Marple continuation novel, must have been a more difficult undertaking than a new Hercule Poirot; furnished by Christie with a cartoonist’s worth of exaggerated traits, the Belgian detective is surely easier to bring off the page than the unassuming but observant elderly spinster. Foley makes a commendable attempt, removing Miss Marple from the postwar austerity of St Mary Mead to the comparative luxury of the Swiss Alps. Although we are introduced to the unnamed body in the gondola cabin at the start, an immediate backward shift for a two-day lead-up means Miss Marple has little actual detecting to do until about halfway through the proceedings. Employing four narrators rather dilutes things, as well as necessitating a considerable amount of Murder of Roger Ackroyd-style withholding of information, but Foley’s Miss M shows her true colours when – of course – the hotel gets cut off from the outside world, and provides a solution worthy of the Queen of Crime herself.

The Silent Appeal by Janice Hallett (Viper, £20)

Bestseller Hallett’s latest novel reunites us with amateur dramatic group the Fairway Players, first encountered in her debut novel, The Appeal. This time the play is The Hollow, dramatised by Agatha Christie from her novel of the same name, and, as before, lawyers Charlotte and Femi are called upon to review the mountain of emails, online messages and police reports through which the story is told, in order to figure out exactly what happened. All we know at the start is that “a brutal murder was committed” and Hallett slowly but expertly ratchets up the tension as clashes over casting, power plays, marital suspicions and distrust of newcomers create an entire gallery of potential murderers and murderees. The epistolatory method may not be for everyone, but Hallett excels at the form – these missives are variously funny, sinister, heartfelt and thoroughly human in their relatable pettiness – and the plot is well up to her usual standard.

Cold Sunset by William Boyd (Viking, £20)

Boyd’s third novel to feature British travel-writer-cum-spy Gabriel Dax takes place in 1964. Initially on the trail of a wartime double agent for the Soviet Union, who operated out of Bletchley Park, our man is then sent to Moscow in order to exfiltrate repentant double agent Kit Caldwell, who promises to offer up secrets in return for sanctuary back in Blighty. Naturally, none of this goes according to plan … Boyd is an accomplished storyteller, excellent on period detail and often funny – the dinner party of self-important Hampstead literati is particularly good – and one can’t help taking proprietorial pleasure in seeing Dax’s tradecraft gradually improving, although he remains alarmingly in thrall to his MI6 handler and on/off lover, Faith Green, who continues to run rings round him. I’d recommend reading this superb series in order.

The Occidental Book of the Dead by T Geronimo Johnson (Abacus, £25)

Taking place in a lightly fictionalised version of Atlanta, Georgia, the central storyline in this wide-ranging juggernaut of a third novel seems superficially straightforward. In 2005, after 13 years in the police force, Black officer George Washington Jonson finds himself in hot water when his redneck rookie partner shoots and kills a white teenager. In due course, a film version of this event and its aftermath serves up an acceptable narrative about racism and corruption. But in the second half of the book, hero-of-the-hour Jonson gives us his own version of the story, which the film-makers told faithfully “except for that fairytale series finale and a couple other facts Hollywood found inconvenient”. The truth, which is much more complex, is a lot less comfortable: internalised racism, overlapping identities, double standards and the sheer messiness of people’s lives are laid bare in an immersive and thought-provoking read.

The Last Tenant by Eva Björg Ægisdóttir, translated by Victoria Cribb (Orenda, £9.99)

The final book in Ægisdóttir’s award-winning Forbidden Iceland series sees Detective Elma Jónsdóttir investigating the case of two skeletons – a woman and a baby, buried some years apart – which have been discovered at a long-abandoned farmhouse in the country outside Akranes, the small west coast town where she works. The farmer who owned it had a reputation for cruelty, but he is long dead, and his son never returned to claim the place. Elma tries to find answers, but is distracted by problems at home – might her partner be having an affair? Meanwhile, single mother Karitas and her young son, Bessi, are in Akranes for a fresh start, but her eccentric landlord’s behaviour is becoming disturbing. Missing family members, people living with past trauma, and the insidious damage caused by secrets abound in this atmospheric and powerful novel.

entries.title: Can’t Get You Out of My Head by Michael Cragg review – what’s the secret of Kylie’s genius?
entries.summary: The pop star emerges as a great unifier in this in-depth yet heartfelt portrait of an Aussie icon‘There’s an anxiety in declaring oneself a Kylie fan,” wrote the late San Francisco poet Kevin Killian (who nonetheless once published an entire collection devoted to the singer). Despite her remarkable longevity, with record-breaking chart success across five decades, Kylie’s place in the pop firmamen
entries.content:
‘There’s an anxiety in declaring oneself a Kylie fan,” wrote the late San Francisco poet Kevin Killian (who nonetheless once published an entire collection devoted to the singer). Despite her remarkable longevity, with record-breaking chart success across five decades, Kylie’s place in the pop firmament has often felt more precarious than that of other artists, perhaps because of her past as a soap star, and the schmaltz of some of her early material with Stock Aitken Waterman.

But she has always displayed a canny self-awareness, alongside a willingness to push the envelope. It’s evident in her knowing rendition of I Should Be So Lucky as a bad poem at the Royal Albert Hall in 1996, and her many collaborations with experimental dance producers. Then there’s her instinct for giving fans what they want: inarguable bangers, like those of her 2000s imperial phase, that also possess an offbeat, idiosyncratic quality, true of Can’t Get You Out of My Head and of her 2023 viral hit, Padam Padam.

Michael Cragg’s illuminating new book explores Kylie’s multiple selves, her talent for shapeshifting, and the question of why she has been persistently underrated. He makes the case that the most easily maligned aspects of her music – frivolity without subtext, fun without an underlying seriousness – are precisely what makes it so pleasurable and available for camp reclamation, its apparent disposability capable of being recast as a virtue.

The Aussie girl next door is thus a different kind of gay icon to club kid Madonna, a grittier figure who looms large here, and whose own acts of reinvention have been considered not just the work of an entertainer, but of an auteur. This comparison is also a matter of taste, of course; in a particularly juicy quote included in the chapter on Kylie’s appeal among gay audiences, singer Rufus Wainwright describes her “as the anti-Madonna. She is what she is and there is no attempt to make quasi-intellectual statements to substantiate it. She is the gay shorthand for joy.”

As to what makes a gay icon, Cragg nimbly tackles the question by including a committee of different voices on the subject, just as he threads his chapters through with interviews. These generate intriguing discoveries and esoteric insights from people as diverse as textile designers, academics and film-makers, all of whose work has been informed by Kylie in some way. While this can slightly disrupt the flow of the book, it also captures the communal ethos that is key to fandom.

Cragg’s prose is appealingly breezy, its register more Popjustice than Pitchfork, but never less than earnest. This project is unambiguously the work of a superfan and scholar of pop, for whom the question of Kylie’s legacy is a high-stakes one. His book is animated by a level of devotion that may not be unique to queer culture, but is certainly one of its hallmarks. There are many reasons we worship our icons in precisely the ways we do, and Cragg’s personal disclosures about his mental health, his early experiences of the closet, and his relationship with his husband provide a touching backdrop to this portrait of why Kylie matters. As does the section reflecting on Kylie’s breast cancer, how it humanised her in the public eye, fostering greater awareness of the disease and underlining the importance of early screening.

That an artist like this has the ability to bring people together might seem like an obvious point, but Cragg urges us not to underestimate “what an amazing service that is”. I finished his book with a newfound appreciation not only of her artistry, but of what she has meant to so many people. She is a singer whose generosity and mutability has allowed her fans to feel whatever they need to feel, nowhere more so than when she performs All the Lovers at her live shows, and arms sway in unison, the song’s lyrics capacious enough for multiple readings, about the adversities of queer life and all of those we have loved and lost.

entries.title: Yellow Dog by Martin Amis review – Bill Nighy has a ball
entries.summary: From spoof monarch to porn tycoon, the actor narrator goes to town on the larger-than-life characters in this Booker-nominated satire In the 2003 novel Yellow Dog, Xan Meo is set upon by two men in a pub who cosh him over the head: “Like the statue of a fallen tyrant, he crashed sideways into the damp paving, and lay still.” Meo is a writer and actor whose late father was a dangerous gangster; the
entries.content:
In the 2003 novel Yellow Dog, Xan Meo is set upon by two men in a pub who cosh him over the head: “Like the statue of a fallen tyrant, he crashed sideways into the damp paving, and lay still.” Meo is a writer and actor whose late father was a dangerous gangster; the attack is in revenge for Meo naming an old associate of his father in print. Meo survives, though the injury leaves him with an altered personality. Where he was previously a conscientious husband and father, now he is a chip off the old block.

While Meo languishes in hospital, King Henry IX – who is struggling to conceal his boredom with the job – is informed that images of his 15-year-old daughter in the bath are in circulation. And Clint Smoker, star reporter and gossip peddler at the tabloid newspaper the Morning Lark, gets an unexpected tipoff.

Yellow Dog is the Booker-nominated satirical novel by Martin Amis which, through a trio of interconnected comic narratives, explores the baser instincts of men. It is one of several Amis titles being released on audio this year; others include Money, London Fields, Night Train and The Rachel Papers.

Bill Nighy is The Yellow Dog’s narrator, and he has a ball voicing Amis’s larger-than-life protagonists. Along with Meo, Smoker and King Henry, a suitably eccentric supporting cast includes Russia, Xan’s long-suffering wife; gruff bodyguard Mal Bale; pornography tycoon Cora Susan; and mercurial football striker and tabloid darling Ainsley Car. Though some of these characters veer into caricature on the page, Nighy succeeds not only in making them believable but great fun to be around.

Available via Vintage Digital, 11hr 54min

Further listening

Love Lane

Patrick Gale, Tinder, 7hr 53min

Gale’s follow-up to his 2015 novel A Place in Winter finds his elderly protagonist Harry Cane sailing home to a radically different England and trying to reconnect with the family he abandoned. Read by the author.

Honoured

Naz Shah, Weidenfeld & Nicolson, 7hr 13min

The Labour MP for Bradford West narrates her memoir recalling her traumatic childhood and teen years – she witnessed domestic violence against her mother and was forced into marriage at the age of 15 – and her eventual path into politics.

entries.title: Exit Party by Emily St John Mandel review – alternate visions of post-crisis America
entries.summary: Is the price of stability necessarily the loss of freedom? Two possible future worlds are linked in the new novel from the author of Station ElevenIn her second novel, 2009’s The Singer’s Gun, Emily St John Mandel tells the story of Anton Waker, a young man desperate to make a break from his criminal family. His plans are thwarted by his cousin Ari, whose hard-nosed talent for operating outside th
entries.content:
In her second novel, 2009’s The Singer’s Gun, Emily St John Mandel tells the story of Anton Waker, a young man desperate to make a break from his criminal family. His plans are thwarted by his cousin Ari, whose hard-nosed talent for operating outside the law has become a way of life. A decade later in The Glass Hotel, a painting called Swan Dive that hangs in the lobby of the luxury retreat stands as a symbol of escape from a trap that is closing. You will not need to have read either of these earlier novels to enjoy Mandel’s seventh, Exit Party, though their loose intertwining of narrative threads will provide extra pleasure and a sense of homecoming for those who have. It is also interesting to observe Mandel’s evolution from a writer of quirky tales of offbeat protagonists to a novelist whose world-spanning, politically resonant narratives now attract a wide and devoted following.

Exit Party begins five years into our future, in 2031. Ari Waker has just come out of prison after serving an 18-year sentence for the attempted murder by contract killing of her cousin Anton. Much has changed while she has been inside: a second civil war has devastated lives and blighted the economy, and the United States as such has ceased to exist.

As the novel opens, the newly inaugurated independent State of California is celebrating the end of violence and the lifting of curfews. Ari and her flatmate Gloria have been invited to a party at the home of Gloria’s friend, Kareem. Ari has the feeling that she is meant to be there; she has experienced such premonitions before, and learned to trust them. Arriving at Kareem’s home, she has the sense that something strange is happening. A woman she’s never met before addresses her as Ibari – the name that is legally hers but never used. A painting disappears from the wall. Someone else talks of “extra people” and of the party being “a door that swings both ways”. “There’s something wrong with this party,” mumbles Kareem, before stepping out into the night and walking away.

Kareem never returns. But Ari does not have time to dwell on the incident. Forced back on her own resources, she spends the next few years working menial jobs, all the time with the underlying sense that there is a different future waiting for her, if she can only reach it: “It wasn’t that she thought she deserved more than what she had … it was just that she’d once had a considerable amount of money, her own business, and a beautiful apartment in a tower in New York City”. Old habits die hard, and it is not long before Ari falls back into criminal company. She is offered a surveillance job – she has always been attracted to detective work – but when the woman she is spying on turns out to be the doppelganger of Gloria, her former flatmate, Ari can no longer ignore the sense of deja vu that has begun to plague her life.

Ari’s world is fractious and chaotic, characterised by scarcity, systemic instability and the ravages of climate change. While her ability to adapt to every situation has enabled her to survive, it has also prevented her from making lasting attachments, a fact she recognises but cannot bring herself to regret. Gloria’s doppelganger Nico speaks of a different world, in which Ari’s own doppelganger Ibari is a high-ranking detective in a government secret police force known as Service.

In this other world, Nico was a physicist, part of a team conducting experiments into teleportation. She was also a dissident. In the novel’s second half, B-Side, we enter a United States where environmental catastrophe has been averted and resources are equitably distributed. It is also a society ruled by universal surveillance, in which the presidency is passed from father to son and where anyone veering from the established order is quietly disappeared.

This is a peaceful dystopia, its glittering streetscapes and self-styled progressivism more reminiscent of Huxley’s Brave New World than Orwell’s concrete-and-jackboots Nineteen Eighty-Four. It is an eerie place, nonetheless. “I studied History before I came to Service,” Ibari says when asked why she decided to serve the lawmakers. “It made me terrified of discord.” While Ibari – reticent, calculating, a loyal arm of Service – might seem to be the polar opposite of the fiercely driven, anarchic Ari, the two women ultimately prove themselves capable of similar acts of recklessness and similar loyalty.

Is the price of stability necessarily the loss of freedom? The question plays out daily in our political reality, its fictional possibilities providing inspiration for writers from Plato’s time onwards. The “upbeat-downbeat” ending Mandel chooses for her novel is not new in science fiction; indeed, it bears comparison to her own earlier take on the post-catastrophe novel, the 2014 blockbuster Station Eleven. What makes Exit Party a superlative example of the form is its structural cohesiveness, its expert play of signs and symbols, its psychological realism. Mandel’s imaginative landscapes have from the first been intricately constructed, an elegant dance in which plot, character and idea appear effortlessly matched. In Exit Party, her ability to handle a complex array of material while never once allowing her focus to drift from the human story reaches new heights.

What does the stolen painting Swan Dive represent? Freedom? Risk? A doomed plunge towards self-destruction? In one particular, irrecoverable moment, Mandel memorably demonstrates how by the end of this extraordinary novel it will have come to mean all three.

entries.content:
This year’s Booker prize shortlist features some very familiar names – previous winners Marlon James and Douglas Stuart are in the running once more, along with Pulitzer winner Elizabeth Strout and prominent British speculative fiction writer M John Harrison.

Novelist and poet Luke Kennard and debut novelist Rebecca Perry are also in contention for the £50,000 prize, the winner of which will be announced on Monday 9 November.

James, the Jamaican writer who took home the prize in 2015 for A Brief History of Seven Killings, was shortlisted this time for The Disappearers. Set in Aids-era Jamaica, the novel centres around an attack on a group of queer men rehearsing John Herbert’s prison-set play Fortune and Men’s Eyes. Coming in at 640 pages, it’s the longest on the list.

Stuart won in 2020 for Shuggie Bain; this time, he’s nominated for John of John, which tells the story of John-Calum Macleod’s homecoming to the Outer Hebrides. The book is an “ardent exploration of the half-lives of queer men condemned to love, pine and suffer in silence”, wrote Yagnishsing Dawoor in a Guardian review.

Strout, who won the 2009 Pulitzer prize for her novel Olive Kitteridge, was previously longlisted for the Booker in 2016 for My Name is Lucy Barton, and shortlisted in 2022 for Oh William! This year, she is shortlisted for The Things We Never Say, which departs from the well-known cast of characters in her previous novels to introduce the history teacher Artie Dam, whose comfortable life on the Massachusetts coast is threatened by a secret, and by the realities of a changing US.

Harrison, who judged the prize in 2022, is shortlisted for The End of Everything, a post-apocalyptic novel set in an unnamed Kent coastal town. The book, “as its title suggests, is about everything”, wrote Michel Faber in the Guardian. “It burrows deep into our psyches – into the psyche of our civilisation – and exposes the terrifying insecurity of life right now.”

The shortlisted books “took risks”, and they “could not be replicated by artificial intelligence – these are very human books”, said the writer Raymond Antrobus, who is on this year’s judging panel alongside the chair Mary Beard, Pulp frontman Jarvis Cocker, the writer Patricia Lockwood, and Guardian journalist Rebecca Liu.

Kennard made the list for Black Bag, his comic campus novel about an actor in his late 30s who takes a job involving attending lectures in a black leather bag as part of a psychological experiment.

Completing the shortlist is Perry, the sole debut novelist, with May We Feed the King. The book – which won this year’s Waterstones debut prize – is about a modern-day curator tasked with dressing rooms in historic houses, who becomes increasingly obsessed with the life of a medieval king.

Four of the shortlisted titles are by men, and three of them – Black Bag, The Disappearers, and John of John – explore masculinity and male sexuality. That the shortlisted authors are predominantly male is “quite surprising, because generally speaking the male-written books weren’t as good as the ones written by women”, said Cocker. The masculinity theme may come down to men “having to rethink their role”, he added. Beard said she doesn’t think it’s a “very masculine” shortlist, while Lockwood half-joked that “all these books are gay”.

Among the surprises on the shortlist was the absence of American author Emma Cline, whose novel Switzy, which follows a man suffering from dementia travelling to a euthanasia clinic, received positive reviews across the board, amid predictions that it could win the overall award. British author Gwendoline Riley also failed to make the cut with her longlisted novel The Palm House.

The judges said the shortlisting meeting lasted approximately three hours. The five other books that didn’t make the shortlist were The Shadow of the Object by Chloe Aridjis, Helen of Nowhere by Makenna Goodman, The Renovation by Kenan Orhan, All Them Dogs by Djamel White, and The Vivisectors by Missouri Williams.

This year’s prize was open to books published in the UK or Ireland between 1 October 2025 and 30 September 2026.

Last year’s prize was awarded to David Szalay for his novel Flesh. Recent winners include Samantha Harvey for Orbital, Paul Lynch for Prophet Song, and Shehan Karunatilaka for The Seven Moons of Maali Almeida.
